source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The Extended Mind
finding: Founding case. Inga recalls from memory that MoMA is on 53rd Street. Otto has Alzheimer's and reads the address from his notebook. They say Otto believed it before he looked, because the notebook plays the same role as Inga's memory.
numbers: One thought experiment; no data. Twin Otto has a notebook that wrongly says 51st Street and so believes 51st.
quote: the notebook plays for Otto the same role that memory plays for Inga
limits: Philosophical argument, not an experiment. Rests on functionalism.
agent_relevance: A notes file or library counts as part of the agent's memory only if it is used like memory. This gives a test for the design.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The Extended Mind: the parity principle
finding: Parity principle: if a part of the world works like a process we would call cognitive if it were in the head, it is part of the cognitive process. It is a test of function, not of location.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: If, as we confront some task, a part of the world functions as a process which, were it done in the head
limits: Parity is a judgement call ('no hesitation'). Critics say it begs the question about what counts as cognitive.
agent_relevance: Use parity as a design check: would we call this step 'memory' if the model did it internally? If yes, treat the store as part of the agent and hold it to the same rules (G2, G3).

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The Extended Mind: conditions for the notebook to count
finding: Four conditions for a store to count as belief-like: (1) constant in the person's life, (2) directly and easily available, (3) automatically endorsed on retrieval, (4) consciously endorsed in the past. They call (4) arguable and say the first three matter most.
numbers: Four criteria; criterion 4 is flagged as arguable.
quote: What is central is a high degree of trust, reliance, and accessibility.
limits: Criteria are qualitative. Automatic endorsement is risky for an agent: it is the same property that lets a wrong note poison later steps.
agent_relevance: Maps to memory design: the library should be always loaded or one cheap call away, but automatic trust must be limited by a check (G3). Entries written by the agent itself and checked count; unchecked entries should not.

source: Clark and Chalmers (1998) The Extended Mind: Tetris, language, social extension
finding: Cites Kirsh and Maglio's Tetris study: turning a piece with the button is far faster than mental rotation, and such moves are called epistemic action. Also says language is a main way cognition is extended, and that another person (a close partner) can play the notebook's role.
numbers: Physical rotation about 100 ms plus about 200 ms to select the button; mental rotation about 1000 ms (as quoted in the paper).
quote: Language appears to be a central means by which cognitive processes are extended into the world.
limits: Numbers are quoted from Kirsh and Maglio, not measured here. See the epistemic-action folder (03) for the full study.
agent_relevance: Cheap external moves can beat internal computation. For the agent: write and run, rather than think, whenever a tool step is cheaper than reasoning. Shared notes between agents are a social-extension case.

source: Wilson and Foglia (2011/2017) Embodied Cognition, SEP: Adams and Aizawa on coupling and content
finding: Adams and Aizawa's coupling-constitution fallacy: a causal link between a process and a tool does not make the tool part of the process. Bowling example: the ball's spin couples with the alley and pins, but spin does not extend into the pins. Their first mark of the cognitive is intrinsic (non-derived) content; notebook entries have only derived content.
numbers: No numbers. Two objections: coupling-constitution; mark of the cognitive.
quote: cognitive states must involve intrinsic, non-derived content
limits: Replies in the entry: causal connection plus functional role is the claim, not coupling alone; Adams and Aizawa 2010 answer that processes without intrinsic content are non-cognitive.
agent_relevance: The critic's line fits our scaffold: a notes file is derived content until the model reads it. The scaffold should not count stored text as knowledge until it is checked and used.

source: Wilson and Foglia (2011/2017) Embodied Cognition, SEP: Rupert, embedding versus extension
finding: Rupert says cognitive systems are embedded in tool-rich settings, not constituted by them. Axe analogy: a person does not become part of the axe. Embedding is 'significantly less radical' and explains the same data. He also argues the Otto and Inga processes differ too much for one science. Clark replies that the brain is 'cognitively impartial' about where operations happen.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: does not care how and where key operations are performed
limits: The data (offloading, notes) fit both readings, so the debate is not decided by experiment.
agent_relevance: For engineering the debate does not matter much: both readings say design the notes loop well. The embedding view warns that a tool is not automatically as reliable as the model's own memory.

source: Wilson and Foglia (2011/2017) Embodied Cognition, SEP: Wilson wide computationalism, Shapiro
finding: Wilson (2004) argues by long multiplication: working on paper is easier than in the head, so computation can be spread across head and paper (wide computationalism). Shapiro answers that parity arguments rest on functionalism, which says bodies do not matter, and that clashes with embodied cognition.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Entry text read to character 100000 of 114500; the last part was not read. Wilson 2004 book itself not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that a scaffold that moves steps onto paper (files, tables, code) changes the computation, not only the storage.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026) Extended mind thesis: Clark 2008 reply to Adams and Aizawa
finding: Adams and Aizawa (2010) raise three objections: causal-constitutional fallacy, cognitive bloating (cognition would cover the whole Internet), coarse-grained functionalism. Clark (2008, Supersizing the Mind) answers: coupling is necessary but not sufficient; the part must play a functional role; being neural is not required. Later moderate versions stress complementarity of inner and outer parts.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, not the primary books. Clark 2008, Wilson 2004, Adams and Aizawa 2001 and Rupert 2004 themselves were NOT opened this session (publisher paywalls).
agent_relevance: Complementarity (inner and outer parts do different jobs) is the useful form for design: the model reasons, the file stores and checks.

source: Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory, Science 333:776
finding: Four studies. Hard questions primed computer-related words. When people expected future access to information, they recalled the information less and recalled where to find it better.
numbers: Exp 1 (Google Stroop): N=46 US undergraduates, 16 easy and 16 hard trivia questions then colour naming (N from the Hesselmann 2020 comparison table). Exp 2 and 3: statements typed to be saved or erased; recall higher in the 'erased' groups and recall of folder location higher (details from secondary reports, not full text).
quote: when people expect to have future access to information, they have lower rates of recall of the information itself
limits: Abstract and secondary accounts only; full Science text not opened. Small samples. Stroop part failed to replicate (see a10, a11).
agent_relevance: Transactive-memory effect: an agent with a reliable library may store 'where' rather than 'what'. Our library should index pointers and store summaries, and be tested for retrieval, not recall.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015
finding: 21 high-powered preregistered replications. Sparrow 2011 was among them and its Google Stroop result did not replicate (reported by Hesselmann 2020).
numbers: 13 of 21 (62%) significant in the same direction; mean replication effect size about 50% of original; sample sizes about 5 times the originals; estimated true-positive rate 67%.
quote: We find a significant effect in the same direction as the original study for 13 (62%) studies
limits: Only the abstract page was opened (paywalled). The per-study Sparrow numbers were taken from the Hesselmann 2020 paper. Original author said design differed (Sparrow 2018 correspondence).
agent_relevance: Treat priming-style 'Internet in the mind' claims as unproven. The transactive-memory recall effects were not what was replicated.

source: Hesselmann (2020) No conclusive evidence for a Google Stroop effect, PeerJ
finding: Second try at Sparrow Exp 1 with a design closer to the original. No priming of Internet words after hard questions. Sequential Bayes factor favoured the null.
numbers: N=117 tested, N=89 in the final sequential Bayes analysis; mean RT hard blocks 825 +/- 453 ms (general words) vs 821 +/- 379 ms (computer words); BF01 = 5.07 for the null. Camerer replication had N=104 (+130 more per the table).
quote: no conclusive evidence in favor of the notion that the concept of the Internet
limits: BF01 of about 5 is moderate, not strong. Only Exp 1 tested; the 'where, not what' recall effect was not.
agent_relevance: The priming half of Google effects is weak. Do not build design on it.

source: Storm and Stone (2015) Saving-enhanced memory, Psychological Science
finding: Saving one file before studying a new file improved memory for the new file. Effect gone when saving was unreliable or the saved content was too small to interfere.
numbers: Three experiments (sample sizes not read).
quote: saving provides a means to strategically off-load memory onto the environment
limits: Abstract only. Later work (PubMed list) tests it with working-memory capacity, partial saving and EEG, mixed support.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for 'offload to free capacity': writing notes before a new subtask frees context. It works only if the save is trusted.

source: Gilbert, Bird, Carpenter, Fleming, Sachdeva and Tsai (2020) Optimal use of reminders, JEP:General
finding: People offload too often. Given a choice between full reward on unaided memory and lower reward with reminders, they chose reminders more than was optimal, even with pay at stake. The bias tracked underconfidence in own memory and vanished with metacognitive advice.
numbers: Three experiments (sample sizes not read from the abstract).
limits: Abstract only. Bias not wholly metacognitive error.
agent_relevance: A model may also over-use its notes or tools. Add a rule that compares expected gain of a lookup to its cost, with a measured confidence.

source: Sachdeva and Gilbert (2020) Excessive use of reminders, Registered Report
finding: Registered report. Paying for performance reduced the offloading bias but did not remove it, so effort avoidance adds to underconfidence.
numbers: Rewarded group vs flat-pay group; sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Offloading is partly effort-avoidance. A token-cheap agent will do the same: prefer the note over thinking when thinking is costly.

source: Risko and Gilbert (2016) Cognitive Offloading, Trends in Cognitive Sciences
finding: Defines cognitive offloading as using physical action to cut mental demand. Asks what triggers it and what it costs. Proposes a metacognitive account: choices follow beliefs about effort and performance.
numbers: Review; no numbers in the abstract.
quote: use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task so as to reduce cognitive demand
limits: Abstract only; full review not opened.
agent_relevance: The metacognitive trigger is the key idea: when to write and when to rely on memory should depend on a measured signal.

source: Toward a metacognitive account of cognitive offloading (2015), physical rotation studies
finding: People rotate their body when text is rotated. But their pattern of rotating did not follow the real performance gains. It followed their rating of the expected benefit.
numbers: Costs of word rotation and frame rotation varied independently; numbers not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Offloading is guided by belief, not measured benefit. Calibrate the agent's belief using measured checks.

source: Fisher, Goddu and Keil (2015) Searching for explanations, JEP:General
finding: Searching the web for explanations raised people's self-rated knowledge. They mistook access for understanding, even rating fMRI images of their own brains as more active.
numbers: Nine experiments reported.
limits: Abstract only. This tests the cost, not the extended-mind claim itself.
agent_relevance: Illusion of knowledge risk: an agent that reads from a library may report the content as its own knowledge. Keep source tags on every retrieved item.

source: Dahmani and Bohbot (2020) Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory, Scientific Reports
finding: More lifetime GPS use went with worse self-guided navigation. In a three-year follow-up, more GPS use predicted steeper decline. GPS use was not explained by poor sense of direction.
numbers: 50 drivers cross-sectionally; 13 retested after 3 years. Lifetime GPS hours vs probe-trial performance r=-0.22 (95% CI -0.41 to -0.01); both probes r=-0.20 (CI -0.41 to 0.01). GPS use vs sense of direction r=0.07.
limits: Small sample, correlational, 13 in the longitudinal part.
agent_relevance: Offloading can decay the internal skill. If the agent is meant to improve its own reasoning, rely on tools for storage but not for the core inference.

source: Gong and Yang (2024) Google effects on memory: meta-analytical review, Front Public Health
finding: Random-effects meta-analysis of Google effects. Pooled effect described as moderate and significant. Effects larger with mobile phones, with low prior knowledge, and in North American samples.
numbers: 908 records screened, 22 articles kept, 35 independent comparisons, 30,889 participants; Cohen d from -0.85 to 4.38; cognitive-load subgroup 0.73 (95% CI 0.22 to 1.24).
limits: Low quality: wide range of d, pooled value not extracted, no publication-bias test seen. Treat with caution.
agent_relevance: Weak support only. Heterogeneity is large.

source: Grinschgl and Neubauer (2022) Supporting cognition with modern technology, Front AI
finding: Review of offloading studies and an outlook on AI. Offloading raises immediate performance but may harm the person's own abilities. Trust in AI relates to personality.
numbers: Review; includes own data on personality and trust in AI.
limits: Perspective paper; sample numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Benefit-risk framing for a tool-using agent: gain now, loss of skill later.

source: Clark (2025) Extending minds with generative AI, Nature Communications 16:4627
finding: Applies the extended mind to LLMs. Argues generative AI can extend thought if trust is calibrated and the interaction is a well-shaped loop. Names the real risks as unreliable stores and misleading output. Cites Digital Andy (retrieval-augmented ChatGPT on his own writings) and FunSearch as examples.
numbers: Commentary; no new data. Cites a Go-player study (more novel human moves after superhuman AI).
quote: we both trust and question the suggestions of the more personalized resource
limits: Opinion piece. Empirical claims are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Supports: build trust-and-question loops (G3), keep the store personal and current, and teach reliability estimates.

source: Clark (2025): metacognition as the skill of choosing what to rely on
finding: Says the practical question is when to rely on bio-memory or on tools: reliability, cost, fragility. Gives examples such as a 15-digit sequence versus a short one.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: skills of knowing what to rely upon and when
limits: Argument, not tested.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema idea of a measured rule for lookup vs recall.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT, arXiv 2506.08872 (preprint)
finding: Essay writing with an LLM, a search engine, or no tool. EEG connectivity fell with the amount of outside help. LLM users had the weakest networks and could not quote their own essays.
numbers: 54 participants in sessions 1-3 (18 per group), 18 in session 4. Quoting failed for 83.3% (15 of 18) of LLM users vs 11.1% (2 of 18) for both search and brain-only (pairwise p<.001). Full ownership: brain-only 16/18, LLM 9/18 in session 1.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Small sample, one task, one city. EEG interpretation is contested.
agent_relevance: Strongest AI-era evidence of offload cost: output not written by the agent is not retained. If the agent writes its own notes, the notes carry the memory.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025): session 4 crossover
finding: Swapping tools in session 4: LLM-to-brain users showed weaker alpha and beta connectivity; brain-to-LLM users showed higher recall and wider activation, like search users.
numbers: 18 participants completed session 4 (9 per switch).
limits: Small crossover sample; no behavioral effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Order matters: think first, then use the tool. Use external help after the agent has formed its own attempt.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents, arXiv 2304.03442
finding: Memory stream of notes with reflection and planning. Ablations show the notes and reflections raise believability.
numbers: 100 human raters ranked 5 conditions. TrueSkill: full architecture mu=29.89 (sigma 0.72); no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; human crowdworkers 22.95; no memory, planning or reflection 21.21. Full vs fully ablated d=8.16. Kruskal-Wallis H(4)=150.29, p<0.001.
limits: Believability ranking by raters, not task accuracy. Rater panel was US-based Prolific workers.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of external notes as agent memory. The reflection layer adds beyond raw storage.

source: Packer et al. (2023) MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems, arXiv 2310.08560
finding: The model pages its own memory in and out of context through function calls. Gain on deep memory retrieval across five prior sessions.
numbers: DMR accuracy: GPT-3.5 Turbo 38.7% to 66.9% with MemGPT; GPT-4 32.1% to 92.5%; GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% to 93.4%. ROUGE-L GPT-4 0.296 to 0.814.
limits: Own benchmark built with an LLM-generated question set. Nested key-value task: only MemGPT worked beyond 2 nesting levels, but plain GPT-4 Turbo was stronger as a baseline.
agent_relevance: A self-managed note store is a working Otto. Accuracy gain is large when the baseline loses old sessions.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion, arXiv 2303.11366
finding: Agent writes verbal reflections after failures into an episodic memory and reuses them. Self-reflection beats keeping only the last trajectory.
numbers: HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0% vs GPT-4 80.1%; MBPP Python 77.1 vs GPT-4 80.1; AlfWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks; HotPotQA ablation: reflection adds 8% absolute over episodic memory of the last trajectory.
limits: On MBPP Python Reflexion did not beat GPT-4 (77.1 vs 80.1). Gains rely on test-case feedback (G2). Memory limited to a sliding window. Table column alignment read from PDF text; check against paper.
agent_relevance: Notes help when they hold real failing output and a lesson. Matches G2.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager, arXiv 2305.16291
finding: Skill library of verified code stored outside the model. Without it, progress plateaus in later stages.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior state of the art.
limits: Minecraft only. Ablation is shown as curves; exact ablation numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: A stored, verified skill library is the strongest case for external memory as a constituent of competence.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval, arXiv 2410.10813 (ICLR 2025)
finding: Benchmark for chat-assistant memory: extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge update, abstention. Long context and memory systems both lose accuracy.
numbers: 500 questions. Long-context LLMs drop 30% to 60% from oracle (evidence only) to the full history: GPT-4o 0.870 oracle vs 0.606 (30.3% drop); Llama 3.1 70B 0.710 vs 0.454 (36.1%) as read from the table.
limits: Synthetic chat histories. Temporal reasoning is weak for retrieval.
agent_relevance: Shows that a note store has to be indexed and queried well. Storing is not enough.

source: Direct input variables: limits of the extended mind within predictive processing (2026), Frontiers in Psychology
finding: A new argument. Outside input can be used as a 'direct input variable' given a probability, without being part of the mind. This drops the reliability and accessibility conditions of the original argument. Mentions Clark 2025 on LLMs.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Philosophy; one author's argument. Read from the PMC full text.
agent_relevance: Suggests treating retrieved text as an input with a probability attached, not as a belief. This fits G5.
